common_name: Sarah Eve Virginia Sweetspire (Narrow-Leaf Native Shrub with Wine-Red Fall Color)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this selection tolerates both boggy sites and average garden soil once roots are established.

directions: A University of Georgia selection distinguished from other Virginia sweetspire cultivars by its narrower, more refined foliage and outstanding burgundy-wine fall coloration that persists later into the season than most forms. Fragrant white bottlebrush racemes appear in late spring on a naturally compact, upright-suckering plant well suited to smaller borders and rain gardens. Best fall color develops with several hours of direct sun; deep shade shifts foliage toward muted maroon. Adapts to average, wet, or occasionally dry soils and tolerates brief flooding, making it a versatile choice for stream banks and low spots.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; keep evenly moist through the first growing season.

directions: An older, densely branched dwarf selection of native summersweet that stays noticeably tighter and more rounded than the species without the need for pruning, making it useful for foundation plantings and small shrub borders. Upright spikes of small, intensely fragrant white flowers open in mid- to late summer and draw abundant bees and butterflies when little else is blooming in the shade garden. Foliage turns clear yellow in fall. Like other clethras it tolerates wet, poorly drained soils and light salt exposure, and spreads slowly by suckers to form a low colony over time.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Scarletta Dwarf Leucothoe (Compact Red-New-Growth Dog Hobble)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mulch with pine bark or pine needles to help maintain soil acidity.

directions: A compact, dwarf sport of drooping leucothoe selected for glossy new spring growth that emerges bright scarlet-red before maturing to dark green, followed by rich burgundy-purple winter color. The arching, layered habit and small stature make it easier to place in foundation and woodland-edge plantings than the larger species. Small, urn-shaped, fragrant white flowers dangle beneath the branches in late spring. Needs consistently moist, acidic soil and protection from hot afternoon sun and drying winds, which can scorch the evergreen foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in average to rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; established plants tolerate heavy shade and dry spells better than most broadleaf evergreens.

directions: A green-leaved, non-variegated Japanese aucuba cultivar prized for its distinctly narrow, coarsely and sharply toothed leaf margins, giving the plant a more textured, willowy look than the plain species. Female plants produce clusters of bright red berries in winter when a male aucuba is grown nearby for pollination. This selection is a reliable, low-maintenance filler for the deepest, driest shade under mature trees where few other broadleaf evergreens perform, and its solid green foliage reads calmer in the landscape than the many speckled gold-dust selections. Protect from harsh winter sun and wind in the coldest part of its range to prevent leaf scorch.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Woodland Ruby Florida Anise (Compact Dark-Red-Flowered Native Shade Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to consistently damp soil in partial to full shade; water regularly during the first two seasons to establish the root system.

directions: A Gulf Coast native evergreen selection of Florida anise chosen for a more compact, densely branched habit than the species along with abundant, deep maroon-red, star-shaped spring flowers held close against the glossy, aromatic foliage. Like other Florida anise selections it thrives in the moist, shaded ravines and stream banks typical of its native range and makes an excellent unclipped evergreen screen or specimen under high pines. All parts have a spicy fragrance when crushed and are not palatable to deer. Consistent soil moisture produces the densest, most floriferous plants; avoid hot, dry, exposed sites.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Michael Lindsey Sweetshrub (Fragrant Deep-Maroon-Flowered Carolina Allspice)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: A named selection of native Carolina allspice chosen for consistently strong fragrance and deep maroon-red flowers, addressing the variability in scent intensity found in seed-grown sweetshrub. The strap-petaled, many-tepaled spring flowers carry a fruity, wine-and-strawberry perfume, and the glossy dark green leaves turn clear yellow in fall. Grows as a dense, rounded, multi-stemmed woodland-edge shrub that suckers moderately to form a naturalistic colony over time. Because fragrance can vary even among named cultivars grown from cuttings of the original plant, source from a reputable propagator when scent is the priority.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
JC Raulston Arboretum at NC State University

common_name: Ellen Huff Oakleaf Hydrangea (Cold-Hardy Large-Panicle Native Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; provide afternoon shade in the Deep South to prevent leaf scorch.

directions: A native oakleaf hydrangea selection noted for improved cold-hardiness of its flower buds along with large, elongated panicles of white flowers that age to soft pink and finally papery tan, held well above the coarse, lobed foliage. The deeply cut, oak-shaped leaves turn deep bronze-red to maroon in fall, giving strong multi-season interest in a shaded border or woodland-edge planting. Like other oakleaf hydrangeas it flowers on old wood, so pruning should be limited to shaping immediately after bloom. Best sited with morning sun and afternoon shade and mulched to keep roots cool and evenly moist.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Haas' Halo Smooth Hydrangea (Native Lacecap Wild Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, average to rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; cut stems back hard in late winter since flowers form on new wood.

directions: A wild-collected native selection of smooth hydrangea valued for its distinctive lacecap flower form, with a flat ring of large, showy sterile white florets surrounding a central dome of small fertile flowers — a striking departure from the mophead 'Annabelle' type more commonly grown. Blooms open in early summer on strong stems and hold up well without flopping. Because it flowers on new wood, it can be cut back close to the ground each late winter to renew the plant and control size. Straightforward in average garden soil and tolerant of a wide pH range, it is an easy, adaptable native for woodland-edge and shaded perennial borders.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Fiber Optics Buttonbush (Dwarf Fine-Textured Native Wetland Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; ideal for pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay damp.

directions: A dwarf, fine-textured selection of native buttonbush with narrow, thread-like leaves that give the whole plant a soft, airy, almost feathery appearance quite unlike the coarse-leaved species. It still produces the signature spherical, pincushion-like white flower clusters in summer that are magnets for bees, butterflies, and other pollinators. Its compact size makes it far easier to place in a residential rain garden or pond edge than standard buttonbush, which can reach small-tree size. Like the species it tolerates standing water and periodic flooding, and it also adapts to average moist garden soil once established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
